evidence_notes.note: Hartley’s body being found at the foot of the stairs is inconsistent with how he actually died: the rigor pattern indicates death occurred while seated or prone on a flat surface, not crumpled from a stair tumble. This strongly supports deliberate staging rather than an accident. The note that the body was moved about two hours after death indicates someone had access and time to reposition him after he expired, which fits a perpetrator who remained in or returned to the workshop. This clue undercuts “fell down the stairs” as a primary cause and instead points to a planned killing followed by concealment.

The absence of traumatic injuries consistent with a fall removes the most obvious explanation for a staircase death. The sallow skin tone and fixed, dilated pupils are described as consistent with systemic poisoning rather than blunt trauma, steering the cause of death away from impact and toward ingestion of a toxin. Combined with the staged placement of the body at the stairs, this clue supports that the fall scene was manufactured after the fact. It also narrows the likely “means” to poisoning, making later evidence about contaminated drink and timing highly probative.

The awl stamped “T.B.” (Thomas Beal’s mark) appears placed beside the body, yet it has no blood and there is no wound consistent with an awl. The board explicitly concludes it was planted and not used. This indicates an intentional attempt to frame or at least misdirect investigators toward Beal by associating his identifiable tool with the death scene. The planting is consistent with a killer who both knew the tool’s ownership would implicate Beal and had opportunity to position it after the killing. It therefore supports consciousness of guilt and a cover story layered on top of the true cause (poisoning).

The wine glass on the workbench contains antimony residue (tartar emetic), and the concentration relative to remaining volume is consistent with a lethal oral dose administered in a single sitting. The board’s estimate that death would follow six to eight hours after ingestion provides a workable window for when the poisoning occurred and when Hartley would succumb. This is the most direct physical evidence of the murder method and ties the death to drinking wine at the workshop rather than to violence at the staircase. It also supports premeditation: antimony had to be introduced into a drink Hartley would consume.

A wine bottle hidden on a shelf behind the tool rack bears a private merchant’s seal and a distinctive yellow delivery ribbon, explicitly noted as not standard shop stock and therefore a special order. Its concealment (hidden shelf) suggests the bottle was managed deliberately rather than being ordinary workshop refreshment. The unusual seal and ribbon become identifying markers that can be matched to purchase documentation, allowing the investigation to trace who procured it. This clue bridges the poisoning evidence (contaminated wine) to procurement and planning, enabling attribution to a specific person connected to the special order.

The wine merchant’s ledger records a private-reserve Bordeaux ordered two days earlier by “G. Lunt,” to be delivered to Hartley’s workshop by four in the afternoon on the murder date, paid in cash with no invoice. This connects Lunt directly to the presence of a special-order wine bottle at the workshop and demonstrates pre-arrangement in advance of the death. Cash/no invoice indicates an effort to reduce paper traceability. The delivery timing (by 4 p.m.) places the bottle at the workshop well before evening events, enabling poisoning to be set up ahead of any meeting. This is key attribution evidence pointing to Lunt as organizer.

The partnership deed establishes that Hartley and Lunt jointly own client accounts and commissions, and that solo solicitation of partnership clients is a breach triggering a financial penalty clause. This provides a concrete business motive framework: client-stealing would have significant financial consequences and could provoke serious conflict within the partnership. It also explains why Lunt would be sensitive to any evidence of Hartley diverting clients and why the dispute would be “matters of business,” matching Lunt’s own characterization. While it does not prove the act itself, it substantiates a plausible motive for Lunt to confront Hartley and potentially escalate to lethal action to prevent loss or penalty.

The torn receipt in Lunt’s waste basket bears the same merchant seal and yellow ribbon mark as the bottle found in Hartley’s workshop, and it is dated with a partial amount visible. It is described as Lunt’s copy of the same order, showing he retained documentation tying him to the special bottle. Its presence in his waste basket, torn, suggests an attempt to destroy or hide evidence after the fact, consistent with guilty knowledge. By matching the workshop bottle’s distinctive markers, this clue corroborates the ledger and strengthens the chain of custody from Lunt to the delivered wine implicated in the poisoning.

Beal states he went to the workshop at nine after a bad argument, knocked, and received no answer; he notes the workshop door was open a crack but the staircase door was shut, and he left without entering. This account places Beal near the scene at a specific time but also provides behavior consistent with not engaging in an assault: he called out and left. The mention of the staircase door being shut aligns with the idea that whatever happened was contained away from public view and that the stair area could be manipulated later. On its own it neither proves nor disproves poisoning, but it supports that silence/absence was noticeable at 9 p.m.

When confronted with the planted awl, Beal acknowledges the stamp but explains he left it at the workshop two weeks earlier for Hartley to repair a strap fitting and that Hartley was supposed to return it. He explicitly asserts someone planted it beside the body and repeats that he was never inside the room. This provides an innocent pathway for Beal’s tool to be available for framing without requiring Beal’s presence during the murder. It supports the board’s assessment that the awl was staged and strengthens the interpretation that the killer intentionally pointed suspicion at Beal using a pre-existing workshop item associated with him.

The wine merchant confirms the bottle was a private order not carried as standard stock and that a gentleman came in two days earlier, paid cash, and requested private delivery to Hartley’s workshop by four in the afternoon, giving the name “Lunt. G. Lunt.” This is an independent eyewitness corroboration of the ledger entry, reinforcing that Lunt personally arranged the special bottle and used cash. The private-delivery instruction shows planning and control over where the wine would appear. When paired with the antimony-laced glass found at the workshop, this testimony supports that the ordered bottle was the vehicle for the poison and that Lunt initiated its procurement.

Lunt admits an eleven-year partnership and frames conflicts as merely business matters, claims he was home all evening, and offers no further detail. This functions primarily as a self-serving alibi statement rather than corroboration; it is unverified within the board. The minimization (“matters of business”) sits awkwardly beside documentary evidence showing high-stakes financial penalties for client poaching and beside physical evidence tying him to the special wine. His refusal to add details does not rebut the procurement trail (ledger, receipt, merchant testimony) or the poisoning indicators. As such, this clue is best read as Lunt attempting to distance himself temporally while other evidence links him logistically and materially to the murder setup.

Whitmore states he had a 6 p.m. appointment with Hartley about a commission, left by 7 p.m., and found Hartley in good health and spirits. This anchors Hartley alive and well shortly before the likely poisoning event, limiting the window for administration and supporting that the fatal act occurred later in the evening. It also helps exclude Whitmore as the poisoner during the appointment, since Hartley showed no signs of distress then. In context with the antimony timeline (death 6–8 hours after ingestion) and the staging evidence, this clue supports an evening ingestion followed by later death and subsequent body movement, consistent with a planned meeting scenario.

content.process_explanation: char_lunt, means_poisoned. Lunt had a clear financial motive rooted in the partnership deed’s penalty for solo solicitation, consistent with the timeline claim that he discovered Hartley had been stealing clients. He arranged the method in advance by ordering a private-reserve Bordeaux for delivery to Hartley’s workshop (ledger and merchant confirmation), and his torn receipt matches the distinctive seal and yellow ribbon on the hidden bottle. Hartley was alive and well at 6–7 p.m., then later drank wine containing a lethal single-sitting dose of antimony from the workshop glass, aligning with the six-to-eight-hour fatal window. After death, the body was moved and staged at the staircase; a planted awl sought to misdirect suspicion toward Beal. Whitmore’s visit ends earlier; Beal’s stamped awl is shown to be staged.
